questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The last index is length - 1, and at(-1) also gives the last item. titles[3] does not exist, so it is undefined, not an error.
questions.code:
const titles = ["Buy milk", "Write report", "Call Ada"];
console.log(titles[titles.length - 1], titles.at(-1), titles[titles.length]);
options: Call Ada Call Ada Call Ada

questions.q: What happens when you read titles[10] on an array with 3 items?
questions.explain: Reading an index that does not exist is not an error in JavaScript; it gives undefined. Check for it before using the value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: push/pop work at the end, unshift/shift at the start. pop and shift give back the item they removed.

questions.q: Which method adds an item to the start of an array?
questions.explain: unshift adds to the start and shift removes from the start. push and pop work at the end.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: slice(start, end) copies from start up to, but not including, end. A negative start counts from the end. The original array does not change.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: splice(1, 2) removes 2 items starting at position 1, changes the array, and gives back what it removed.

questions.q: What is the difference between slice and splice?
questions.explain: The names look alike but do very different things. slice never changes the original; splice removes and inserts items in place.
options: They are two names for the same method
slice copies part of the array into a new one; splice changes the original array
slice works on strings only; splice on arrays only

questions.q: You want to change a copy of an array and keep the original as it is. Which line makes that copy?
questions.explain: slice() with no arguments copies the whole array. const copy = list only gives the same array a second name, so changing copy changes list too.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both compare with ===, so case matters: "Urgent" is not "urgent". indexOf gives -1 when the value is missing.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: find gives the first matching item and findIndex its position. With no match, they give undefined and -1.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: some asks "does at least one item match?" (42 does). every asks "do all items match?" (42 does not).
questions.code:
const scores = [42, 87, 65];
console.log(scores.some((s) => s < 50), scores.every((s) => s >= 50));

questions.q: You need the first task whose title is "Call Ada", as an object. Which method fits?
questions.explain: find takes a callback and gives back the first matching item itself. includes and some only answer true or false, and indexOf needs the exact value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: map transforms each item, filter keeps the items whose callback returns truthy, and reduce combines everything into one value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: map, filter and reduce never change the original array. Each gives back something new.

questions.q: What does map always give back?
questions.explain: map keeps the length and replaces each item with what your callback returns. Use filter to keep only some items and reduce for one value.
options: An array with only the items that passed the callback
A new array of the same length, with each item transformed
A single value, such as a total
Nothing; it changes the array in place

questions.q: Why should you always give reduce a starting value, like 0?
questions.explain: With a starting value, the total of an empty list is simply that value, such as 0. Without it, an empty array throws a TypeError.
options: Without it, reduce starts from the first item and throws on an empty array
Because the starting value is added to every item
Because reduce returns an array without it

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With the starting value 0, the empty total is 0. Without it, reduce has nothing to start from and throws a TypeError.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The callback gets the index as a second argument, starting at 0. forEach gives back nothing, so result is undefined. Use it only for side effects like printing.
options:
1. Buy milk
2. Write report
[ 'Buy milk', 'Write report' ]

questions.q: What can a for...of loop do that forEach cannot?
questions.explain: Both run once per item. Only a loop lets you break out early. Pick whichever reads better.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By default, sort converts every item to a string and sorts as text. As text, "100" comes before "25" because "1" comes before "2".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: b - a puts the largest first. toSorted gives back a sorted copy, so the original order is kept.

questions.q: A sort comparator (a, b) => … returns a negative number. What does that mean?
questions.explain: Negative means a first, positive means b first, and 0 means they are equal. a - b therefore sorts numbers from smallest to largest.

questions.q: Which is true about sort and toSorted?
questions.explain: Prefer toSorted unless you really want to change the original. Both take a comparator, and both sort as text without one.
options: toSorted changes the array; sort gives back a copy
sort changes the array; toSorted gives back a sorted copy
toSorted always sorts numbers correctly without a comparator

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The default string order puts all capital letters before all small letters. a.localeCompare(b) sorts text the way a person expects.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each step gives back a new array: clean the words, drop the empty ones, keep only the first appearance of each word, then sort. join glues them into one string.

questions.q: Why can you chain .map(…).filter(…).toSorted()?
questions.explain: Each method returns an array, so you can call the next method straight on the result. Put each step on its own line so it reads like a recipe.
options: Because each method changes the original array
Because each of these methods gives back a new array, so the next method can be called on it
Because chaining is a special syntax only for arrays of strings

questions.q: Which chain fails with a TypeError?
questions.explain: forEach gives back undefined, so there is no array to call filter on. The other methods all return new arrays.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both names are lower-cased before comparing, so the search ignores case. find returns the whole object, or undefined, which the caller must check for.

questions.q: addStudent("Femi", "88") is rejected with "grade must be 0 to 100". Why is refusing it the right design?
questions.explain: Number.isInteger("88") is false. The function refuses the wrong type instead of guessing, so bad data never ends up in the list.
options: Because 88 is not a valid grade
A grade from a form arrives as text; the caller must convert it with Number, and the function should not guess
Because push cannot add strings to an array
Because names must be longer than four letters

questions.q: Why does averageGrade start with if (students.length === 0) return 0;?
questions.explain: With no students, the total is 0 and the count is 0, and 0 / 0 is NaN. The guard returns a sensible answer instead.
options: To avoid dividing by zero, which would give NaN
Because an empty array has a length of undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Sort a copy by grade, largest first, keep the first two, and format them. Because toSorted makes a copy, the original order is not disturbed.

questions.q: The programmer forgot to check for -1. What does this print?
questions.explain: findIndex gives -1 when nothing matches, and splice(-1, 1) removes the last item. Always check for -1 before using an index.

questions.q: Finish cleanList(words) with a chain: trim and lower-case each word, drop empty ones, drop repeats, and sort. Return the words joined with ", ". The program should print bread, eggs, milk.
questions.explain: Clean first, then filter: empty words only become "" after trimming, and "Milk" only repeats "milk" after lower-casing.

questions.q: Finish passedNames(students) with filter, map and join: return the names of students with a grade of 80 or more, as one comma-separated string. The program should print Ada, Chen.
questions.explain: filter keeps the students who passed, map turns each into its name, and join glues them together.

questions.q: Finish total(prices) with reduce so it adds up the prices. It must return 0 for an empty list. The program should print 5450 0.
questions.explain: Always give reduce a starting value. With 0, an empty list gives 0 instead of throwing.

questions.q: Finish sortedScores(scores) so it returns a new array sorted from smallest to largest, without changing scores. The program should print the sorted copy, then the unchanged original.
questions.explain: Use toSorted so the original is not changed, and pass (a, b) => a - b: without a comparator, numbers are sorted as text.

questions.q: Finish removeStudent(name): remove the student with that name from students and return true, or return false when there is no such student. Use findIndex and splice, and check for -1.
questions.explain: Check for -1 before using the index; splice(-1, 1) would silently remove the last student.

questions.q: Finish addStudent(name, grade). Trim the name. Return "rejected: name is required" for an empty name, "rejected: grade must be 0 to 100" when the grade is not a whole number from 0 to 100, and "rejected: NAME exists" when a student with that name exists (ignoring case). Otherwise push the student and return "added NAME".
questions.explain: Validate first with guard clauses, then save. some answers "does a student with this name already exist?". The string "88" fails Number.isInteger, so it is refused.

added Dayo
rejected: ada exists
rejected: name is required
rejected: grade must be 0 to 100
2

questions.q: Finish averageGrade(students): return 0 for an empty list, otherwise the average grade rounded to one decimal. The program should print 87.3 0.
questions.explain: Guard against the empty list (0 / 0 is NaN), add the grades with reduce, then round: multiply by 10, round, and divide by 10.

questions.q: Use forEach with its index argument to print each title as a numbered line, starting at 1.
questions.explain: The callback's second argument is the index, which starts at 0, so add 1 for a human-friendly number.

questions.q: How do you check whether value is an array?
questions.explain: Arrays are objects, so typeof says "object", and so do plain objects and null. Array.isArray is the reliable check. Strings have a length too.

questions.q: const titles = ["a", "b"]; Which line throws an error?
questions.explain: const only stops the name from pointing at a different array. Changing the array itself (mutating it) is allowed.

questions.q: Which of these methods changes the original array?
questions.explain: splice, push, pop, shift, unshift and sort change the array. map, filter, slice and toSorted give back something new.

questions.q: A list holds the numbers [1, 2, 3]. What does list.includes("2") give?
questions.explain: includes and indexOf use strict comparison. The string "2" is not the number 2. Convert outside input with Number first.
options: A TypeError, because the types differ

questions.q: const student = students.find((s) => s.name === name); What must your code do before reading student.grade?
questions.explain: With no match, find returns undefined, and reading undefined.grade throws a TypeError. It is findIndex that returns -1.
options: Check that student is not undefined, because find gives undefined when nothing matches

questions.q: Finish page(items, pageNumber, size) with slice: page 1 is the first size items, page 2 the next size, and so on. Do not change items.
questions.explain: Page 1 starts at index 0, page 2 at size, and so on. slice copies up to, not including, the end index, stops at the end of the array, and never changes the original.

questions.q: Finish gradeOf(name) with find. Ignore case when matching the name. Return the student's grade, or "not found" when there is no such student.
questions.explain: Lower-case both names before comparing. find returns undefined when nothing matches, so check for it before reading .grade.

questions.q: Process a queue of jobs in order. Use a while loop and shift to take jobs from the start of queue until it is empty, printing done JOB for each. Then print how many jobs are left.
questions.explain: shift removes and returns the first item, so jobs run in the order they arrived. Each call makes the array shorter, which is what lets the loop end.
questions.expected:
done email
done resize
done backup
left: 0
